issues.title: Air conditioning does not cool
issues.blurb: No cold air. Could be a system that has quietly lost its charge, or a compressor that is never being asked to run.
issues.symptom:
Air comes out, but it is not cold. On a car this age that is one of two stories, and they are told apart in about thirty seconds without any tools.

The thirty-second test

Engine running, A/C on, fan on full. Look at the compressor pulley at the front of the engine. Does the centre of the pulley — the clutch plate — snap in and start turning with the belt?

  • It does not engage. The system is not being allowed to run. Almost always low refrigerant: the pressure switch inhibits the clutch to protect the compressor from running dry. Could also be the fuse, relay or amplifier.
  • It engages but the air stays warm. The system runs but is not moving heat — charge, condenser, expansion valve or evaporator.
issues.cause:
The manual's own symptom table puts refrigerant volume first for all three cooling faults — no compressor operation, no cool air, and insufficient cooling. That ordering is not an accident. R134a systems lose a little charge every year through the hose walls and shaft seal, and after twenty years a system that has never been touched is usually simply empty.

The second most likely thing, given the whirr from the glovebox, is that both faults share a cause: a blocked evaporator housing restricts airflow and can mask a system that is actually working. Diagnose the blower first — it is free.

check.t: Does the compressor clutch engage?
check.hint: Watch the pulley centre with A/C on and the fan at full.

check.t: Check the drive belt condition and tension
check.hint: AC-16. A slipping belt looks exactly like a dead compressor.

check.t: Check the A/C fuse and the magnetic clutch relay
check.hint: Relay is in the engine bay box, not the instrument panel J/B.

check.t: Gauge the system for pressure
check.hint: AC-10. Needs a manifold gauge set — this is where DIY usually stops.

check.t: Inspect the condenser for blockage and damage
check.hint: It sits in front of the radiator and collects road debris.

check.t: Check the pressure switch
check.hint: AC-51. This is what inhibits the clutch when the charge is low.

issues.fix:
If it is charge — and it usually is — the honest answer is that a re-gas alone is a temporary fix. The gas left through a leak, and it will leave again. A shop should evacuate the system, hold a vacuum to prove it is sealed, then charge by weight. The compressor condenser and evaporator oil charges are in the manual if anything gets replaced.

Where to stop

Opening a refrigerant circuit without recovery equipment vents R134a to atmosphere, which is both illegal and pointless. Diagnose as far as the clutch test and the visual checks, then hand it to someone with gauges and a recovery machine.

Compressor oil quantities when parts are replaced: 40 cc for a condenser, 40 cc for an evaporator, 120 cc for a compressor. ND-OIL 8 or equivalent.

issues.title: Whirring from behind the glovebox
issues.blurb: That is where the blower motor lives. Almost always debris in the fan cage or a dry bearing — and both are reachable in under an hour.
issues.symptom:
A whirr, hum or rattle from the passenger footwell area. The single most useful observation costs nothing:

Does the noise change with fan speed?
  • Yes — rises and falls with the fan. It is the blower motor or something loose inside its housing. That is this issue.
  • No — constant regardless of the fan, or only with A/C on. Look elsewhere: a belt, an idler, or the compressor itself.

A rhythmic tick or flutter usually means a leaf or a bit of trim caught in the squirrel cage. A dry, even whirr that gets worse with speed usually means the motor bearing.
issues.cause:
The blower sits directly behind the glovebox and draws cabin air through the air refiner filter — which is right there too, and which on a twenty-year-old car is very often clogged or missing entirely. When that filter is gone, everything the intake picks up goes straight into the fan.

The manual's job order tells you how accessible it is: remove the glove compartment parts, disconnect the connector, three screws, and the motor is out. Then it can be tested on the bench with nothing more than a battery and two leads.

check.t: Confirm the noise tracks fan speed
check.hint: Cycle through all speeds with the engine off.

check.t: Pull the air refiner filter and look at it
check.hint: Two pins in the glovebox, pull it down, the filter case slides out.

check.t: Look into the blower housing for debris
check.hint: Leaves and grit collect in the fan cage.

check.t: Spin the blower wheel by hand
check.hint: Roughness or side-play means a worn bearing.

check.t: Bench-test the motor on 12 V
check.hint: AC-48: positive to terminal 1, negative to terminal 2, check it runs smoothly.

check.t: Check the blower resistor while you are in there
check.hint: AC-49: continuity across terminals 1-2-3-4.

issues.fix:
Work through it in the order the access gives you, because each step is free once the glovebox is down:

  1. Air refiner filter. Two pins, glovebox drops, case pulls out. If it is dirty or absent, replace it — that alone fixes a surprising number of blower noises and improves airflow, which matters for the A/C fault too.
  2. Clear the housing. Anything loose in the cage comes out with a vacuum and a careful hand.
  3. Test the motor. If it is rough on 12 V off the car, replace it. Blower motors are not usually worth rebuilding.

Do this before spending anything on the air conditioning. It is the cheapest job on the list and it may change what the A/C fault looks like.

issues.title: Corrosion — bottom of the door
issues.blurb: A little rust along the bottom edge. On a door that is almost always blocked drain holes, which means it is rotting from the inside out.
issues.symptom:
Bubbling or brown staining along the lower edge of the door skin, usually worst at the corners.

What you can see is not the extent of it

A door rusts from the inside. Rain runs down the glass, past the weather strip, into the cavity, and out through drain holes in the bottom edge. When those holes block with road grime the water stops leaving, and the skin corrodes outward from behind the paint. By the time it shows on the outside, the inside is worse.
issues.cause:
Blocked drains, nearly always. Twenty years of grit, and on a lowered car the door bottoms sit closer to the spray.

Worth checking as part of the same job: whether the weather strip at the base of the glass is still sealing, and whether the vapour barrier behind the door trim card is intact. A torn barrier lets water into the cabin side as well.

check.t: Find the drain holes along the bottom edge of the door
check.hint: Poke them clear with a cable tie, not a screwdriver — do not scratch the paint.

check.t: Pour a little water down inside the glass and watch it drain
check.hint: It should run straight out within seconds.

check.t: Press the affected area firmly
check.hint: If it flexes or crunches, the metal behind is gone, not just the paint.

check.t: Pull the trim card and check the vapour barrier
check.hint: BO front door section covers the sequence.

check.t: Check the same spot on the other door
check.hint: Whatever caused it is probably symmetrical.

check.t: Look at the sill under the side skirt
check.hint: Bonded skirts trap water against the sill — see the bodykit mod notes.

issues.fix:
Scale of the repair depends entirely on the press test:

  • Surface only, metal still solid. Clear the drains, cut back to bright metal, treat, etch prime, colour, lacquer, then cavity-wax the inside of the door. This is a home job.
  • Metal perforated. It needs cutting out and letting in. Filler over a hole buys one winter and makes the eventual repair bigger.

Clear the drains whatever you do. Repairing the skin without fixing the drainage just resets the clock.

MOT note

A door skin is not a structural member, so surface corrosion here is not an automatic failure. Corrosion within 30 cm of a structural mounting point is a different matter — which is why the sill underneath the skirt is worth a look at the same time.

issues.title: Corrosion — tailgate at the wing mounts
issues.blurb: Rust around where the GT wing bolts through the tailgate skin. This one has an obvious cause and an obvious lesson.
issues.symptom: Corrosion breaking out around the wing's mounting points on the tailgate.
issues.cause:
Every hole drilled through a painted steel panel exposes bare edge metal. Unless that edge is sealed on both faces, water wicks in around the fastener, sits between the wing foot and the paint, and corrodes outward from the hole. A rubber gasket under the wing foot holds the water in rather than keeping it out.

This was predictable, and it is on the mods page

The GT wing dossier already flags it: "Every new hole through the tailgate skin is a corrosion start point. Seal both faces and cavity-wax the inside." That is what has happened. The same warning applies to the tail bar project, which cuts a 1.1 metre aperture in the same panel — worth getting the method right on this repair first.

check.t: Remove the wing and look at the panel underneath
check.hint: The visible rust is the edge of it, not the whole of it.

check.t: Check inside the tailgate around each hole
check.hint: Trim board off. Corrosion from a drilled hole works both ways.

check.t: Check the tailgate drain paths are clear
Look at the glass flange and the lower edge while it is apart
Decide whether the wing goes back on the same holes
check.hint: Repairing around existing holes is harder than filling them and starting again.

issues.fix:
1. Wing off, panel cleaned back to bright metal around every hole.
  2. Treat, etch prime, and — the step that gets skipped — seal the bare edge inside each hole, not just the visible face.
  3. Colour and lacquer, then cavity-wax the inside of the tailgate.
  4. Refit on new fasteners with a sealant bead under each foot, not a bare rubber pad.

Added mass high on the tailgate also works the gas struts harder — worth checking they still hold the panel up while it is all apart.

issues.title: Missing exhaust heat shield
issues.blurb: Came off and has not been replaced. Those shields are not decoration — they keep exhaust heat off the floor pan and everything routed near it.
issues.symptom:
A shield departed some months ago. First job is working out which one, because the car has several and they matter to different degrees.

Two families of shield
  • Exhaust manifold heat insulators — upper and lower, bolted to the manifold in the engine bay. These are the ones that crack around their bolt holes from heat cycling and fall off. The 2ZZ-GE runs hot and this is common.
  • Underfloor heat insulators — panels between the exhaust and the floor pan. The manual's exhaust system page shows four of them.
issues.cause:
Thin stainless, hundreds of heat cycles, and captive nuts that rust. The shield cracks around a fastener, starts to rattle, and eventually leaves.

Consequences, in order of how much they should worry you: heat into the floor pan and whatever is routed along it; degraded underseal and sound deadening above the exhaust; a rattle that sounds much more expensive than it is; and — if it is a manifold shield on a lowered car with a bodykit — more under-bonnet heat than the engine bay was designed to shed.

check.t: Get the car up and identify which shield is missing
check.hint: Look for empty captive nuts or torn mounting tabs.

check.t: Check the remaining shields for cracks around the fixings
check.hint: If one went, its neighbours are the same age.

check.t: Look at the floor above where the shield should be
check.hint: Discoloured or blistered underseal means it has been getting hot.

check.t: Check nothing else has been heat-damaged
check.hint: Brake lines, fuel lines and wiring routed along the tunnel.

check.t: Check for a rattle at idle and on the overrun

issues.fix:
Replace it. These are cheap parts and there is no good reason to run without one.

If the mounting tabs have rotted away, a stainless repair strap and an exhaust clamp is an accepted fix — but it has to be metal. Cable ties near an exhaust are a fire, not a repair.

FasteningN·mkgf·cmft·lbf
Upper heat insulator × exhaust manifold — 2ZZ-GE2020415
Lower heat insulator × exhaust manifold — 2ZZ-GE2020415
Exhaust manifold × cylinder head — 2ZZ-GE5051037

Read off SS-14 (p.164) and the 2ZZ-GE manifold installation procedure (p.894). The 2ZZ lower insulator takes four bolts, the upper five.

issues.title: Engine oil and filter due
issues.blurb: Overdue on a lift engine is not the same as overdue on an ordinary one — the VVTL-i lifters are hydraulic, and oil is what operates them.
issues.symptom:
Nothing wrong yet. This one is on the list because of what the engine is.

Why the 2ZZ-GE cares more than most

Lift is engaged by oil pressure pushing a locking pin through a slipper follower. Low, thin or degraded oil means the pin does not lock reliably — and a lift mechanism that half-engages at 6,200 rpm is how these engines destroy a lobe. The usual first symptom is lift that comes in late, inconsistently, or not at all when hot.
issues.cause: Ordinary service interval. Worth doing more often than the book implies on an engine that spends time near 8,000 rpm.

check.t: Check the level on a warm engine, parked level
check.hint: Do this far more often than you change it.

check.t: Look at the colour and feel of the oil
check.hint: The manual says to replace it if the quality is visibly poor, regardless of mileage.

check.t: Note the mileage and date before draining
check.hint: Log it in the garage page afterwards.

check.t: Check whether this car has an oil cooler
check.hint: It changes the fill quantity — 4.4 L with, 4.2 L without.

check.t: Have a new drain plug gasket ready
check.hint: The manual calls for a new one every time.

issues.fix:
Straight out of the manual's own procedure:

  1. Remove the centre engine under cover.
  2. Remove the oil filler cap, then the drain plug, and drain into a container.
  3. Replace the oil filter. Toyota specify SST 09228-06501, and to tighten the new filter a further 3/4 turn after the gasket contacts.
  4. Clean and install the drain plug with a new gasket.
  5. Refill, run, check for leaks, re-check the level.
ItemFigure
Drain plug torque37 N·m — 378 kgf·cm, 27 ft·lbf
Capacity, with oil cooler4.4 L — 4.8 US qt, 4.0 Imp qt
Capacity, without oil cooler4.2 L — 4.6 US qt, 3.8 Imp qt
Dry fill4.8 L — 5.1 US qt, 4.2 Imp qt
GradeAPI SJ / ILSAC, SAE 5W-30 named first choice

Torque and procedure read off LU-3 (p.1070); capacities off PP-17 (p.75). The 5W-30 recommendation is the manual's, written in 1999 — plenty of 2ZZ owners run a heavier grade in summer, which is a judgement call, not a specification.
